docs.text: Artificial Intelligence for Geospatial Applications Build AI and deep learning solutions for Earth observation — from classical machine learning to foundation models, segmentation, and deployment on maps and dashboards. Item Detail Category Certificate Course Level Certificate / intermediate-to-advanced Course fee 5,800 ETB Processing fee 200 ETB Total 6,000 ETB Modules 11 Lessons 11 Knowledge checks 33 questions React preview /courses/ai-geospatial Course guide Artificial Intelligence for Geospatial Applications is a certificate / intermediate-to-advanced programme built around 11 practical modules. Work through the modules in order; each one includes objectives, notes, a hands-on exercise, a knowledge check, and a deliverable. Learning outcomes Use training and test data and feature engineering to work with foundations of ai and machine learning for geospatial data and explain the result. Use electromagnetic spectrum and platform and sensor characteristics to work with preparing satellite and aerial imagery for model training and explain the result. Use training and test data and feature engineering to work with classical ml: random forests, gradient boosting, and svms with scikit-learn and explain the result. Use Earth Engine data catalog and ImageCollection filtering to work with deep learning with pytorch and tensorflow for image classification and explain the result. Use convolutional feature learning and encoder-decoder segmentation to work with semantic segmentation using u-net and vision transformers and explain the result. Use training and test data and feature engineering to work with object detection for infrastructure and land features and explain the result. Prerequisites Comfort with files, folders, and basic data tables. Introductory knowledge of the relevant tool or programming language. Willingness to complete short practical exercises after each module. Full module documents Module 01 — Foundations of AI and machine learning for geospatial data Learning objectives Explain foundations of ai and machine learning for geospatial data and where it fits within Artificial Intelligence for Geospatial Applications. Use scikit-learn or Earth Engine classifiers and training samples to complete a small, documented workflow. Validate the result, record assumptions, and communicate the main finding clearly. Key concepts training and test data feature engineering model selection validation metrics Lesson notes Foundations of AI and machine learning for geospatial data is best learned as a repeatable workflow: state the question, prepare the inputs, apply the method, check the output, and communicate the result. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are training and test data, feature engineering, model selection. Use scikit-learn or Earth Engine classifiers to demonstrate the idea, and use training samples to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Never evaluate a model on the same data used to train it; use a held-out test set or cross-validation. Hands-on exercise Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for foundations of ai and machine learning for geospatial data. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with scikit-learn or Earth Engine classifiers: prepare labelled samples, train two models, compare confusion matrices, and explain which model is preferable. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. Knowledge check Show questions and answers 1. **What is overfitting?** Answer: When a model learns training noise and performs poorly on unseen data. 2. **What does a confusion matrix show?** Answer: Correct and incorrect counts by class, enabling precision, recall, and accuracy calculations. 3. **Why are training samples important?** Answer: They define what the model learns; biased or mixed samples produce unreliable predictions. Deliverable A one-page practical note containing the question, data description, method steps, one output, and three bullet points of interpretation. Module 02 — Preparing satellite and aerial imagery for model training Learning objectives Explain preparing satellite and aerial imagery for model training and where it fits within Artificial Intelligence for Geospatial Applications. Use a satellite scene viewer and band combinations and spectral indices to complete a small, documented workflow. Validate the result, record assumptions, and communicate the main finding clearly. Key concepts electromagnetic spectrum platform and sensor characteristics spatial/spectral/temporal resolution image interpretation Lesson notes Preparing satellite and aerial imagery for model training is best learned as a repeatable workflow: state the question, prepare the inputs, apply the method, check the output, and communicate the result. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are electromagnetic spectrum, platform and sensor characteristics, spatial/spectral/temporal resolution. Use a satellite scene viewer to demonstrate the idea, and use band combinations and spectral indices to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Do not compare images from different dates or sensors without checking calibration, cloud cover, and spatial resolution. Hands-on exercise Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for preparing satellite and aerial imagery for model training. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with a satellite scene viewer: compare at least two band combinations, label three land-cover features, and explain how resolution affects interpretation. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. Knowledge check Show questions and answers 1. **What does spatial resolution describe?** Answer: The ground size of one pixel; smaller pixels mean finer spatial detail. 2. **Why are near-infrared and red bands useful for vegetation?** Answer: Vegetation strongly reflects near-infrared and absorbs red, making their contrast useful for vegetation indices such as NDVI. 3. **What should be checked before comparing two satellite images?** Answer: Date, sensor, calibration, cloud cover, projection, and spatial resolution. Deliverable A one-page practical note containing the question, data description, method steps, one output, and three bullet points of interpretation. Module 04 — Deep learning with PyTorch and TensorFlow for image classification Learning objectives Explain deep learning with pytorch and tensorflow for image classification and where it fits within Artificial Intelligence for Geospatial Applications. The central ideas in this lesson are Earth Engine data catalog, ImageCollection filtering, cloud masking and compositing. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. Deliverable A one-page practical note containing the question, data description, method steps, one output, and three bullet points of interpretation. Module 05 — Semantic segmentation using U-Net and Vision Transformers Learning objectives Explain semantic segmentation using u-net and vision transformers and where it fits within Artificial Intelligence for Geospatial Applications. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are convolutional feature learning, encoder-decoder segmentation, data augmentation. Use PyTorch or TensorFlow to demonstrate the idea, and use labelled image tiles to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Check for train/validation leakage caused by overlapping tiles from the same scene. Hands-on exercise Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for semantic segmentation using u-net and vision transformers. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with PyTorch or TensorFlow: prepare a small tile dataset, train or fine-tune a compact model, inspect predictions, and compute IoU. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. Knowledge check Show questions and answers 1. **What does a U-Net architecture do?** Answer: It combines a contracting encoder with an expanding decoder and skip connections for pixel-level prediction. 2. **Why augment training images?** Answer: To improve generalisation by exposing the model to rotations, flips, brightness changes, and crops. 3. **What does IoU measure?** Answer: The overlap between predicted and reference shapes divided by their union. docs.text: Data preparation and augmentation for satellite imagery is best learned as a repeatable workflow: state the question, prepare the inputs, apply the method, check the output, and communicate the result. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are electromagnetic spectrum, platform and sensor characteristics, spatial/spectral/temporal resolution. Use a satellite scene viewer to demonstrate the idea, and use band combinations and spectral indices to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Do not compare images from different dates or sensors without checking calibration, cloud cover, and spatial resolution.
docs.title: Lesson notes

docs.text: Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for data preparation and augmentation for satellite imagery. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with a satellite scene viewer: compare at least two band combinations, label three land-cover features, and explain how resolution affects interpretation. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps.
docs.title: Hands-on exercise

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What does spatial resolution describe?** Answer: The ground size of one pixel; smaller pixels mean finer spatial detail. 2. **Why are near-infrared and red bands useful for vegetation?** Answer: Vegetation strongly reflects near-infrared and absorbs red, making their contrast useful for vegetation indices such as NDVI. 3. **What should be checked before comparing two satellite images?** Answer: Date, sensor, calibration, cloud cover, projection, and spatial resolution.

Learning outcomes Use climate indicators from space and time-series anomaly detection to work with climate change indicators from space and explain the result. Use convolutional feature learning and encoder-decoder segmentation to work with urban expansion and impervious surface mapping and explain the result. Prerequisites Comfort with files, folders, and basic data tables. Introductory knowledge of the relevant tool or programming language. Willingness to complete short practical exercises after each module. The central ideas in this lesson are convolutional feature learning, encoder-decoder segmentation, data augmentation. Use PyTorch or TensorFlow to demonstrate the idea, and use labelled image tiles to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Check for train/validation leakage caused by overlapping tiles from the same scene. Hands-on exercise Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for urban expansion and impervious surface mapping. Apply the main technique with PyTorch or TensorFlow: prepare a small tile dataset, train or fine-tune a compact model, inspect predictions, and compute IoU. Knowledge check Show questions and answers 1. **What does a U-Net architecture do?** Answer: It combines a contracting encoder with an expanding decoder and skip connections for pixel-level prediction. 2. **Why augment training images?** Answer: To improve generalisation by exposing the model to rotations, flips, brightness changes, and crops. 3. **What does IoU measure?** Answer: The overlap between predicted and reference shapes divided by their union. docs.text: Vegetation health monitoring (NDVI, EVI time series) is best learned as a repeatable workflow: state the question, prepare the inputs, apply the method, check the output, and communicate the result. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. Use Google Earth Engine Code Editor or rgee to demonstrate the idea, and use ImageCollection filters to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Unfiltered ImageCollections can be very large; always limit date, region, and bands before running expensive operations.

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **How do you reduce an ImageCollection to one image?** Answer: Use a reducer such as median, mean, or qualityMosaic over the collection. 2. **Why is cloud masking important?** Answer: Clouds and shadows distort spectral values and can lead to false change or index results. 3. **What should be specified when exporting an Earth Engine result?** Answer: Region, resolution or scale, projection/CRS, file format, and asset or drive destination.

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What does a U-Net architecture do?** Answer: It combines a contracting encoder with an expanding decoder and skip connections for pixel-level prediction. 2. **Why augment training images?** Answer: To improve generalisation by exposing the model to rotations, flips, brightness changes, and crops. 3. **What does IoU measure?** Answer: The overlap between predicted and reference shapes divided by their union.

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What is the difference between vector and raster data?** Answer: Vector data use points, lines, and polygons; raster data use a grid of cells or pixels. 2. **Why must layers share a CRS before analysis?** Answer: Otherwise distances, areas, and overlays are computed in incompatible coordinate systems. 3. **What does a clip operation do?** Answer: It extracts the part of one layer that falls inside the extent of another layer.

Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are vector and raster data models, coordinate reference systems, spatial queries and overlays. Use QGIS or GeoPandas to demonstrate the idea, and use a CRS transform to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Always confirm the CRS before measuring distance or area; degrees are not metres.
docs.title: Lesson notes

docs.text: Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for geopandas for vector data analysis. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with QGIS or GeoPandas: import two layers, align their CRS, run a buffer or clip operation, and produce a labelled map with a legend and scale bar. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps.
docs.title: Hands-on exercise

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What is the difference between vector and raster data?** Answer: Vector data use points, lines, and polygons; raster data use a grid of cells or pixels. 2. **Why must layers share a CRS before analysis?** Answer: Otherwise distances, areas, and overlays are computed in incompatible coordinate systems. 3. **What does a clip operation do?** Answer: It extracts the part of one layer that falls inside the extent of another layer.

Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are Earth Engine data catalog, ImageCollection filtering, cloud masking and compositing. Use Google Earth Engine Code Editor or rgee to demonstrate the idea, and use ImageCollection filters to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Unfiltered ImageCollections can be very large; always limit date, region, and bands before running expensive operations. Hands-on exercise Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for gee account setup and code editor tour. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with Google Earth Engine Code Editor or rgee: filter an ImageCollection by date and region, apply a cloud mask, calculate an index, and export a small result for validation. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. Knowledge check Show questions and answers 1. **How do you reduce an ImageCollection to one image?** Answer: Use a reducer such as median, mean, or qualityMosaic over the collection. 2. **Why is cloud masking important?** Answer: Clouds and shadows distort spectral values and can lead to false change or index results. 3. **What should be specified when exporting an Earth Engine result?** Answer: Region, resolution or scale, projection/CRS, file format, and asset or drive destination. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. Knowledge check Show questions and answers 1. **What does spatial resolution describe?** Answer: The ground size of one pixel; smaller pixels mean finer spatial detail. 2. **Why are near-infrared and red bands useful for vegetation?** Answer: Vegetation strongly reflects near-infrared and absorbs red, making their contrast useful for vegetation indices such as NDVI. 3. **What should be checked before comparing two satellite images?** Answer: Date, sensor, calibration, cloud cover, projection, and spatial resolution. docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **How do you reduce an ImageCollection to one image?** Answer: Use a reducer such as median, mean, or qualityMosaic over the collection. 2. **Why is cloud masking important?** Answer: Clouds and shadows distort spectral values and can lead to false change or index results. 3. **What should be specified when exporting an Earth Engine result?** Answer: Region, resolution or scale, projection/CRS, file format, and asset or drive destination.

Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are vector and raster data models, coordinate reference systems, spatial queries and overlays. Use QGIS or GeoPandas to demonstrate the idea, and use a CRS transform to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Always confirm the CRS before measuring distance or area; degrees are not metres. Hands-on exercise Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for urban planning fundamentals with gis. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with QGIS or GeoPandas: import two layers, align their CRS, run a buffer or clip operation, and produce a labelled map with a legend and scale bar. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. The central ideas in this lesson are vector and raster data models, coordinate reference systems, spatial queries and overlays. Use QGIS or GeoPandas to demonstrate the idea, and use a CRS transform to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Always confirm the CRS before measuring distance or area; degrees are not metres.
docs.title: Lesson notes

docs.text: Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for creating and sharing maps. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with QGIS or GeoPandas: import two layers, align their CRS, run a buffer or clip operation, and produce a labelled map with a legend and scale bar. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps.
docs.title: Hands-on exercise

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What is the difference between vector and raster data?** Answer: Vector data use points, lines, and polygons; raster data use a grid of cells or pixels. 2. **Why must layers share a CRS before analysis?** Answer: Otherwise distances, areas, and overlays are computed in incompatible coordinate systems. 3. **What does a clip operation do?** Answer: It extracts the part of one layer that falls inside the extent of another layer.

docs.text: Spatial analysis and mapping techniques is best learned as a repeatable workflow: state the question, prepare the inputs, apply the method, check the output, and communicate the result. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are vector and raster data models, coordinate reference systems, spatial queries and overlays. Use QGIS or GeoPandas to demonstrate the idea, and use a CRS transform to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Always confirm the CRS before measuring distance or area; degrees are not metres.
docs.title: Lesson notes

docs.text: Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for spatial analysis and mapping techniques. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with QGIS or GeoPandas: import two layers, align their CRS, run a buffer or clip operation, and produce a labelled map with a legend and scale bar. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps.
docs.title: Hands-on exercise

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What is the difference between vector and raster data?** Answer: Vector data use points, lines, and polygons; raster data use a grid of cells or pixels. 2. **Why must layers share a CRS before analysis?** Answer: Otherwise distances, areas, and overlays are computed in incompatible coordinate systems. 3. **What does a clip operation do?** Answer: It extracts the part of one layer that falls inside the extent of another layer.

Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are document structure, math typesetting, floats for tables and figures. Use LaTeX to demonstrate the idea, and use a compiled .tex document to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Use labels and cross-references instead of hard-coded numbers so the document stays correct after edits.

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What is the advantage of BibTeX over manual reference lists?** Answer: Citations and the bibliography are generated consistently from one source file. 2. **How are figures usually handled in LaTeX?** Answer: As float environments with captions, labels, and cross-references. 3. **Why avoid hard-coded section numbers?** Answer: LaTeX renumbers automatically; manual numbers become wrong when content changes.

No prior programming experience is required for the introductory lessons. Full module documents Module 01 — MATLAB interface Learning objectives Explain matlab interface and where it fits within Introduction to MATLAB. Use MATLAB to demonstrate the idea, and use built-in numerical functions to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Check vector dimensions and convergence criteria; many MATLAB errors come from shape mismatches or stopping too early. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps. docs.text: Working with vectors and matrices is best learned as a repeatable workflow: state the question, prepare the inputs, apply the method, check the output, and communicate the result. Keep the original data untouched and save each processing step so the work can be repeated. The central ideas in this lesson are vector and raster data models, coordinate reference systems, spatial queries and overlays. Use QGIS or GeoPandas to demonstrate the idea, and use a CRS transform to confirm that the output behaves as expected. Always confirm the CRS before measuring distance or area; degrees are not metres.
docs.title: Lesson notes

docs.text: Write a one-sentence question and define the study area or sample extent for working with vectors and matrices. Prepare the input data and record its source, date, resolution or scale, and coordinate system where relevant. Apply the main technique with QGIS or GeoPandas: import two layers, align their CRS, run a buffer or clip operation, and produce a labelled map with a legend and scale bar. Validate the result visually and numerically; note any unexpected patterns, missing values, or outliers. Export the final map, table, or figure and write a short interpretation with limitations and next steps.
docs.title: Hands-on exercise

docs.text: Show questions and answers 1. **What is the difference between vector and raster data?** Answer: Vector data use points, lines, and polygons; raster data use a grid of cells or pixels. 2. **Why must layers share a CRS before analysis?** Answer: Otherwise distances, areas, and overlays are computed in incompatible coordinate systems. 3. **What does a clip operation do?** Answer: It extracts the part of one layer that falls inside the extent of another layer.
